activities.title: Write the first letter I hear
materials: 3 or 4 small toys (sun, tiger, pig, mouse or others you have)
parentPrompts: Pick up a toy, say its name slowly, and ask: "What sound do you hear first?"
Help them think of a letter that makes that sound (s for sun, t for tiger, p for pig, m for mouse). Say the letter name and write it.
Let them write the first letter for each toy on paper and draw a quick picture of it.
Look for: sensible sounds. If they write a letter you do not expect, ask: "What sound did you hear?" Early spelling by sound is a good sign.

activities.title: Stretch and write words
parentPrompts: Keep small items like buttons, coins, and seeds out of mouths, and stay close while your child plays.
Say the word 'at'. Push one counter forward for each sound: /a/, /t/. Ask: "What letters make those sounds?"
Write 'at' together. Then try 'it' and 'in' the same way.
Add a first sound: put 's' in front of 'at' to make 'sat'. Let them write the s themselves.
Look for: they can hear each sound and write a letter for it. Spelling does not need to be perfect.

activities.title: Draw a picture and write a label
parentPrompts: Ask your child to draw something they know about, like a pet, a tree or a toy.
Ask: "What is this?" and write the word on a sticky note. Let them copy any letters they can, or write the first letter themselves.
Ask them to tell you one more thing about the picture, like "It is soft." Write it down for them.
Look for: a label or letters next to the drawing and a spoken fact about it.

activities.title: Write a sentence with the word I
parentPrompts: Write 'I see a' on a strip of paper. Tell your child: the word I is always a capital letter, and a sentence starts with a capital letter.
Look at a picture or out the window. Ask: "What do you see?" Fill in the blank by drawing it or writing the first letter.
Have them copy 'I see a' under a drawing and complete the sentence with your help. Add a dot at the end and name it: a period.
Look for: capital I, spaces between words, and an attempt to finish the sentence.

activities.title: Make a tiny book about me
materials: 3 sheets of paper folded in half and stapled (adult only)
parentPrompts: Staple the pages into a book (adults only). On the cover, help your child write their name as the author.
On each inside page, they draw one thing they like and write or dictate a word or sentence.
Read the book together at the end. Ask: "Who made this book? Who drew the pictures?" (They did both!)
Look for: a drawing plus some letters or words on each page. Keep the book for the reader time later.

activities.title: Take-away stories
parentPrompts: Put 5 toys on the table. Say: "5 toys are playing. 2 go home." Slide 2 under the cloth. Ask: "How many are left?"
Count what remains. Say it out loud: "5 take away 2 leaves 3."
Try new stories: 4 take away 1, 3 take away 3 (none left!). Let your child hide the toys this time.
Look for: they can say how many are left by counting what remains. Keep stories happy and silly.

activities.title: Two-color counters
materials: 5 small things that are the same on both sides, like 5 pennies (or paper circles colored red on one side)
parentPrompts: Keep small items like buttons, coins, and seeds out of mouths, and stay close while your child plays.
Put 5 counters in a cup, shake and spill. Count how many red and how many other.
Say: "2 red and 3 yellow make 5." Draw it on paper with colored circles.
Do it again 5 or 6 times. Ask: "Can we make 5 a different way?" Find as many pairs as you can: 0+5, 1+4, 2+3, and so on.
Look for: they know each pair adds to 5 and can find at least 2 different ways.

activities.title: Counting to 30 and counting by tens
materials: a counting chart or paper strip 1 to 30 (optional)
parentPrompts: Count out loud to 30 together. Many children skip numbers like 13 or 20; go slowly on those.
Put 10 things in each of the 3 cups. Count by tens as you point to each cup: "10, 20, 30."
Count forward from a given number: "Start at 24 and count up to 30."

Look for: counting through 30 in order without skipping, with some help on teen numbers. Safety: small items are a choking hazard for babies and toddlers, so keep them away from younger siblings and out of mouths.

activities.title: Ten frame with teens
materials: a paper rectangle divided into 10 boxes (2 rows of 5)
parentPrompts: Fill the 10 boxes with counters. Say: "This is ten." Count them.
Add 2 more outside the frame and say: "Ten and two more is twelve." Try 13, 15 and 18.
Ask: "Show me 14." Check that they fill the frame first and then add 4.
Look for: they see that teen numbers are 'ten and some more.' Safety: small items are a choking hazard for babies and toddlers, so keep them away from younger siblings and out of mouths.

activities.title: Review games
parentPrompts: Play three quick games: count out a number card's worth of items; roll or pick two groups and say which has more; and tell a number story together.
Let your child be the teacher for one round and check your work.
End with a victory cheer: count to 30 together.

Look for: which game felt easy and which felt tricky. Repeat the tricky one in a few days, since this is a review. Safety: small items are a choking hazard for babies and toddlers, so keep them away from younger siblings and out of mouths.

activities.title: Two characters, two adventures
parentPrompts: Pick two stories you have read. Recall a character from each.
Ask: "What did each character do? What happened to them?"
Ask: "How are they alike? How are they different?" Draw a heart on what is alike and a star on what is different.
Look for: they can tell something about each character and one way they are alike or different.

activities.title: Join in reading
materials: a book with repeating words or a rhyme
a nursery rhyme or song you both know
parentPrompts: Choose a book with a repeating line. Tell your child: "When we get to the repeating part, you say it with me."
Read it again, pausing so they can fill in the repeating line or the rhyming word.
Switch: you read one page and they say the repeating line. Clap on the beat.
Look for: they join in at the right time and seem to enjoy the sounds.

activities.title: Find the connection
materials: a nonfiction book about plants, weather or animals
parentPrompts: Read a page that talks about two things, like the sun and a plant.
Ask: "How are these two things connected?" Give a sentence starter: "The sun helps the plant because..."
Find another pair in the book, like a bird and a nest. Ask the same question.
Look for: they connect two things in their own words, even simply.

activities.title: Draw and tell about my favorite
parentPrompts: Ask: "What is your favorite book? What is it called?" Write the title at the top of the page.
Ask: "Why is it your favorite?" Write down what they say after 'I like it because...'.
Have them draw a picture of their favorite part. They can add letters or labels.
Look for: they name the book and give a reason. Reasons can be small, like 'it has a dog'.

activities.title: Act out a story
materials: simple props like a scarf or a stuffed animal
parentPrompts: Pick a familiar story. Decide who plays each character. Use a scarf or hat as props.
Retell the story as a play with the beginning, middle and end. You can be the narrator.
Switch roles. Ask: "How does this character feel?"
Look for: events in order, character voices, and a sense of how a character feels.

activities.title: Compare the 3 cups
parentPrompts: Keep small items like buttons, coins, and seeds out of mouths, and stay close while your child plays.
Look at each cup. Ask: "What do you see? Which cup has a sprout? Which has none?" (Seeds can take several days to a couple of weeks.)
Measure any sprout with blocks or by comparing to a finger. Draw what each cup looks like.
Ask: "What did the plant in the light and water have that the others did not?" Plants in the dark may look pale and thin. That is normal.
Look for: they compare the cups and say plants need light and water. Wash hands afterward.

activities.title: Outdoor animal watch
parentPrompts: Go outside and sit quietly for 10 minutes. Look for birds, insects and other small animals. Do not touch animals; some bugs bite or sting. Wash hands afterward.
Ask: "What is it doing? What might it eat? Where does it live?"
Draw one animal and where it was found.
Look for: they can say what the animal needs (like food or a hiding place). Not seeing any is fine; look at the signs, like a nest or a web.

activities.title: Make a poster of what living things need
materials: pictures of plants, animals and people (optional)
parentPrompts: Draw a plant, an animal and a person in three spots on the paper.
Ask: "What does each one need?" Draw lines to pictures of water, food, light or a place to live.
Say: "Plants and animals live where they can get what they need." Ask: "Where would a bird live? A fish?"
Look for: they connect each living thing to its needs and a place it lives. Hang the poster up.

activities.title: Jobs in a place
parentPrompts: Pick a place from earlier lessons (like a library or a store). Ask: "Who works there? What do they do?"
Draw the place and the workers.
Ask: "What job might you like to try someday?"
Look for: they connect jobs to places and say what workers do.

activities.title: Make a community book
materials: 3 sheets of paper folded and stapled (adult only)
parentPrompts: Staple a small book (adults only). On the cover write 'Our Community'.
On each page draw a place, a helper and a rule or kind act from the earlier lessons.
Read the book together. Ask: "What is your favorite page?"
Look for: they can retell something they learned about community and rules.

activities.title: Collage of places and helpers
parentPrompts: Find pictures of places and helpers in your community. Adults cut or the child tears.
Glue them to the large paper to make a collage.
Talk about each one.
Look for: pictures sorted by place or helper. Supervise scissors.

activities.title: Cardboard town
parentPrompts: Decorate boxes to be buildings like a library, a store or a fire station.
Place them on the floor to make a town.
Drive toy cars on roads made of tape.
Look for: they name each building and who works there.

activities.title: Make a card for a helper
parentPrompts: Pick a helper to thank (a mail carrier, a neighbor, a doctor or someone else).
Fold paper into a card, draw a picture, and write 'Thank you' for them to copy.
Have them dictate a sentence to add.
Look for: a card that shows care. Deliver it together if you can.

activities.title: Shaker instrument
materials: an empty plastic bottle with lid
parentPrompts: Put a small handful of rice in the bottle. Glue or tape the lid closed (adult only). Safety: keep the lid taped so contents do not spill.
Decorate the bottle.
Shake to a beat. Play soft and loud.
Look for: a steady beat. Check that the lid stays sealed.

activities.title: Our art gallery
parentPrompts: Hang the art from the unit on a wall or lay it on the floor.
Walk through like a museum. Ask your child to tell about each piece.
Ask: "Which is your favorite? Why?"
Look for: they can describe their art in words. End with a bow.
